posts.body_html:
Hi Mike, my Towns Co. are from elsewhere. That exterior color is insane, is it limited to that single pitcher or is the whole plant coloring like that?

Here's all three of my Blue Ridge Mountains S. oreophila right now:

Left to right: Clay Co., NC; Towns Co., GA no. 2 (the one that infuses pink); Towns Co., GA no. 1 (the one with very reticulated veins.

The Clay Co. plant is kind of perplexing - it's consistently emerged from dormancy pretty much last among my Sarracenia (it didn't start growing up June this year, which is when most of my Alabama S. oreophila are producing phyllodia). The Towns Co. plants continue to excel for me though:


No. 1



No. 2 - colors just starting to infuse


Clay Co. (left) and Towns Co. no. 2 (right) showing the same venation pattern.

posts.body_html:
Pretty much all the oreophilas this season are producing fall colors (eg. turning orangey red). They have stopped producing traps and are now in phyllodia mode, while the old traps are senescing and will turn brown pretty soon. The towns Co, GA population is well known to consistently produce fall colors this time of year, and it does happen in the wild as well but I don't know when as the grow season in GA is much different than here.

posts.body_html:
I don't exactly know how this works, but here's what I suspect: if the summer traps are cleaned up early enough in the season and the growth points receive direct sunlight for a certain period of time during the late summer/early fall, it seems this is what induces fall trap production!

Pics taken 10/28/25: notice only the front row of plants are producing fall traps!

posts.body_html:
So what do those late fall traps look like now that they've had time to age? They're really coloring up! This population is very well known to produce nice colors during late summer as the traps age, so it's no surprise that they're looking really amazing right now! Pics taken 12/10/25:




Look at the trap in the middle left hand corner of the photo with a green stripe through it! That's because there was an old, dead pitcher shading that portion of the trap, I removed it right before taking the photo! Full sun is absolutely necessary to bring out these colors:
